title: anywaye SLI catalogue and label allowlist
description: The allowlist that replaces a shared client library. Six languages write an SLO's two PromQL strings by hand, and the two ways they get it wrong are (a) spelling a metric or a label the collector never writes, and (b) spelling one that means nothing. Neither is visible in review and both are visible only at 3am, as an SLI that reads `no data` and an error budget that never moves. So the SLI is not free text: a metric name in any anywaye SLO must be one this file names, and the names here are the **Postgres-normalized** spellings of the OpenTelemetry attributes and metrics beside them — `service.name` becomes `service_name`, `http.response.status_code_class` becomes `http_response_status_code_class`, and the HTTP duration histogram's series suffix (`_seconds_count`, after the exporter's UCUM translation of `s` to `_seconds`) is part of the name rather than a detail of the query. Handled by a name allowlist rather than a parser, which is what makes this file checkable by a service's own test suite in whatever language it is written in, and by core's harness with the standard library. Three properties: `slis`, the catalogue of SLIs a service may declare, named after the **user-visible operation** and never after a service (a catalogue entry called `identity` would be an SLO for identity written by a spec); `allowedLabels`, the dimensions a query may filter on, which are exactly the measurement attributes `metrics.schema.json` allows with the resource attribute folded in; and `forbidden`, **two separate lists** — unbounded dimensions and infrastructure signals — which are two prohibitions with two reasons and must not be merged into one.

http_server_availability.description: The base every HTTP SLI is built on: requests served without a 5xx. The base is here as its own entry so that an SLO scoped to a *service* is still scoped to something a user can notice — an SLO whose `total_query` is answered by "the service is up" is a chart, not a contract.

otelName.description: The OpenTelemetry semantic-convention metric this is derived from. **Stable**, with recommended bucket boundaries — which is why an HTTP SLI is built on it rather than on a connector's guess at one.

errorOtelName.description: The OpenTelemetry name the bad half is counted under. The same name as `otelName` when one counter serves both halves, which is the usual case for an HTTP availability SLI and the reason it needs no second metric.

totalMetric.description: The histogram's count series: one per request, whatever its outcome.

errorMetric.description: The same series. The error and the total are one counter and a label, which is the whole reason an availability SLI is computable without a second metric and without a message in a label.

http_response_status_code_class.description: A 5xx, not a 4xx: a client sending a bad request is not an outage, and counting it would make the error budget a measure of how many people call the API wrongly.

errorSelector.description: The extra matcher that turns the shared metric into "the bad half". Capped at one matcher, because a second one is how an SLI starts selecting a population nobody agreed to measure.

labels.description: The dimensions this SLI may filter on. `http_route` is the **template** (`/v1/auth/token`), never a concrete path — that is the one value per endpoint rather than one per request, and `metrics.schema.json` already says so.

requiredLabels.description: None. The base SLI is the whole service; narrowing it is what the operation-scoped entries below are for.

description.const: Requests the service handled without a server error, over its whole surface.
description.description: What the SLI promises, in the words a user would use. Required, because an SLI nobody can read is a chart.

authentication_succeeds.description: R6's first candidate: a user can log in. Not "the identity service is up" — an SLI whose total is every request the service ever served can be green while nobody can log in, which is the failure a service-scoped SLO hides rather than catches. `http_route` is therefore REQUIRED: without it this entry is the base SLI wearing a name about authentication.

otelName.description: The same semconv metric. One metric serving two SLIs is normal and cheap; a second metric per SLO is a second thing to emit, keep and trust.

errorOtelName.description: The same name, for the same reason: the bad half of this SLI is the same counter with a 5xx on it.

totalMetric.description: Requests to the authentication route, whatever their outcome.

http_response_status_code_class.description: A 5xx on the authentication route. A 401 is a correct answer to a wrong credential and is not in the numerator — the same rule as everywhere else, and the reason `error_type`'s vocabulary has `policy_denied` in it rather than counting a refusal as an outage.

errorSelector.description: The matcher that turns a request into a failure a user would notice.

labels.description: The same four dimensions as the base. Narrowing by method is allowed; narrowing by anything else is not.

requiredLabels.description: `http_route`, and it is not optional. This is R6 in one constraint: the SLO must name the operation, and the operation is identified by the route template.

description.const: A caller can authenticate: a token request to the named route returns without a server error.

event_accepted_into_outbox.description: R6's second candidate: an event is accepted into the outbox. This is the operation that makes the whole event story honest — `docs/event-outbox.md` promises a write in the same transaction, and this is the SLI that says the promise holds. It counts **publish attempts**, not rows written, because a row that is written and never published is the failure an outbox exists to surface.

otelName.description: anywaye's own OpenTelemetry-shaped name, following the dotted convention `metrics.schema.json` already states for a metric name. anywaye owns this name; a service that declares an SLO on this entry must emit it, which is the next packet's work and is what makes that work mechanical.

errorOtelName.description: A second counter rather than a matcher on the first: a publish that failed is an event that happened, and folding it into the same series as a publish that succeeded would make the error rate depend on a label the collector has to be configured to keep.

totalMetric.description: Publish attempts, success or failure. The denominator is every attempt because an attempt that never happened is not measurable and an attempt that failed is the thing being counted.

errorMetric.description: Attempts that exhausted their retries or were given up on. Carries `error_type`, so the reason is a class from the fleet's vocabulary rather than a free string.

errorSelector.description: Empty, on purpose: the bad half is its own counter here rather than a matcher on a shared one. `maxProperties: 0` is what makes "empty" a decision — an SLI that quietly added a matcher would be measuring a population nobody agreed to.

labels.description: `error_type` on the failed counter, so a ticket says which of the twelve classes fired. No `tenant_id`: a per-tenant publish rate is a per-tenant SLI, which is unaffordable at this traffic level and is barred twice over.

requiredLabels.description: None: the whole publisher, which is the right granularity for an SLI that every publishing service runs the same loop for.

description.const: An event this service accepted is published, rather than sitting in the outbox waiting for someone to notice.
description.description: What the SLI promises, in the words a user of the product would use.

email_dispatched.description: R6's third candidate: an email is dispatched. Dispatched rather than delivered, because delivery is the provider's promise and this fleet does not operate it; an SLO that measured delivery would be an SLO on a vendor's SMTP reputation, which is a metric nobody can page on and every user blames on us.

otelName.description: anywaye's own name, for the same reason as the outbox entry: the operation is named, the emitting service is not.

errorOtelName.description: The refused-or-given-up-on half. `provider_rejected` and `provider_auth` are separate classes on this counter, so a rotated credential and a content-policy refusal are visible as themselves rather than as one undifferentiated "email is broken".

errorMetric.description: Attempts the provider refused or we gave up on. `provider_rejected` and `provider_auth` are separate classes in the vocabulary, so a misconfigured credential is visible as itself rather than as "email is broken".

errorSelector.description: Empty: the bad half is its own counter.

labels.description: No `email` and no address, ever. `metrics.schema.json` prohibits `email` as a measurement attribute for the cardinality reason and the redaction reason at once, and an address in a PromQL selector would put a customer's address in every alert's query string.

description.const: An email the product asked for is handed to a provider without a refusal or a permanent failure.
description.description: What the SLI promises — and, by leaving delivery out, exactly how far it reaches.

invoice_computed.description: R6's fourth candidate: an invoice is computed. The one operation in the fleet where the number itself is the point, which is why it is an SLI rather than a dashboard: a customer's invoice is the artefact, and "it computed" is a thing a user notices. **Money is never a metric**: `metrics.schema.json` has no currency unit for exactly this reason, so both counters below are counts of computations.

otelName.description: anywaye's own name, operation-named like the rest of the catalogue.

errorOtelName.description: A computation that did not produce an invoice. Deliberately not a money amount: `metrics.schema.json` has no currency unit, so nothing about how much an invoice was may become a metric series, and an SLI over a monetary series is a billing dashboard pretending to be a contract.

errorMetric.description: Computations that did not produce an invoice. An invoice that is *wrong* is not in here: counting it would put a business rule in an error budget, and it is fixed by a code change that has its own test.

errorSelector.description: Empty: the bad half is its own counter.

labels.description: No `account_id`, no `customer_id`, no `plan_id`: every one of those is unbounded, every one is already barred as a measurement attribute, and a per-customer invoice SLI is the most tempting and most unaffordable of them all.

requiredLabels.description: None: the whole billing service, because an invoice that is late for one customer because of another customer's plan change is still an invoice that is late.

description.const: An invoice the product owed a customer was computed, rather than failing to compute at all.

slis.description: The closed set of SLIs a anywaye service may declare. Named after the **operation a user can notice**, never after a service or a table, because a catalogue entry that said `identity` would be an SLO for identity written by a specification — and the next packet would inherit a threshold nobody chose.

allowedLabels.description: Every label an SLO query may filter on, in the spelling the collector writes: every measurement attribute `metrics.schema.json` allows, with dots replaced by underscores, plus `service_name`. An SLO whose query names a label outside this list selects a series nothing exports, which Prometheus answers with `no data` — and an SLI that reads `no data` reports an error rate of zero and burns no budget while the service is on fire. An `enum` and not a pattern, because the list is the rule: adding a label to it is a spec change with a test, which is the only way an unbounded dimension gets in.

forbidden.description: Two lists, two reasons, and they are not merged because a reader who is about to add one of these needs the reason, not the verdict.

unboundedDimensions.description: **Reason: cardinality, and it is already decided.** OpenTelemetry caps aggregation at 2000 distinct attribute combinations per metric stream and, on overflow, folds everything into one point and drops every measurement attribute: totals stay right and every breakdown silently undercounts. `metrics.schema.json` prohibits all four as measurement attributes and *requires* `tenant_id` and `account_id` on `resourceAttributes`, which are exempt from the cap. So a per-tenant SLI is not merely discouraged here, it is unreachable — and the honest form of a per-tenant view is a recording rule over the resource attributes, which is an attribution question rather than an SLO.

infrastructureSignals.description: **Reason: an SLO on these is not an SLO.** `cpu`, `memory`, pod churn and restart counts describe the machine the service runs on, not anything a user can notice: a pod restart loop on a service nobody is calling is green in every user-visible measure and red in every infrastructure one. They are also the measures a deployment has to keep well away from its limits, which is a capacity decision with an owner and a lead time — not an error budget. These belong in an alert on a *symptom* the service's own RED metrics show, and in a runbook; they do not belong in the budget a pager spends.

metricName.description: A Postgres-normalized metric name: the OpenTelemetry name with dots replaced by underscores, then the UCUM unit in Prometheus's spelling, then the series type (`_total`, `_count`, `_bucket`, `_sum`). The `not` is the union of the two `forbidden` lists, and it is a second line rather than the rule — it cannot reject a name the `const` beside it accepts, so it can never cause a false rejection. It is here because a `const` is one edit away: the rule that survives someone widening the catalogue is the one that does not depend on the current contents of it.
